what_this_is: The accepted set for tools/history_secrets.py. Every row is a false positive triaged by hand, with the reason stated, so a later reader can disagree with the disposition rather than only with the count.
a_path_row_is_broad: A row keyed on `path` accepts that kind anywhere in that file, in every version of it in history. A row keyed on `object` accepts exactly one blob, which is exactly one set of bytes. Path rows are used here because a placeholder in a register is a different blob in every revision of that register, and an object row per blob would be hundreds of rows that go stale on the next commit. The cost is real: a genuine credential of the same kind, added later to one of these files, would be accepted silently. That is the one way this file can cause harm, and it is why every row names a specific string rather than a category.
never_a_value: Rows describe shapes and name placeholders. Where a row quotes a string, the string is a documented placeholder or a fixture that says so in its own text, never a credential, including a rotated one.

accepted.why: The literal placeholder `postgresql://user:password@host/db` inside an incident narrative about a connection string a shell expansion once printed. The username is the word user and the password is the word password. Triaged in audit-2026-10-15.md.

That audit quoting the same placeholder in order to dispose of it. A security report that names a shape will match a scanner for that shape, and the alternative is a report that cannot say what it looked for.
